lesson_title: The Fifteen Cents That Was Never Yours: VAT
hook_text: Inside every R46 till slip, R6 was never the shop's money. Not for one second.
clip_script: Farida runs a corner shop near the taxi rank. A customer buys a bag of sugar for forty-six rand — and inside that price, exactly six rand is not hers. It never was. It is VAT, riding inside the till slip, and she holds it for SARS the way a taxi conductor holds the fares for the owner. Every sale splits invisibly into two piles: the shop's money, and the tax man's money sleeping in her till until payday. But Farida is also a customer — the wholesaler charged HER VAT on stock, the electrician charged VAT on the rewiring. So every two months, one subtraction: VAT collected from customers, minus VAT she paid out herself. Collected five thousand seven hundred, paid three thousand nine hundred — she owes SARS one thousand eight hundred. And look closer at that number: she bought for twenty-six thousand and sold for thirty-eight — twelve thousand of value SHE added. Fifteen percent of twelve thousand? Exactly one thousand eight hundred. The tax's name is its own explanation. Then her brother-in-law suggests the two-till trick — let the cash sales vanish. Here is why that fails: every invoice her wholesaler issued sits in the wholesaler's OWN return. A shop buying twenty-six thousand of stock and declaring twelve thousand of sales is a red light on a screen at SARS. The two-till shop is not a secret. It is a delayed penalty.
visual_style: A till drawer splitting each note into two glowing piles — shop money and a smaller SARS pile; the two-monthly subtraction drawn as two streams meeting; the brother-in-law's second till flickering red as matching invoices light up on a distant screen.
pacing: Everyday open, clean subtraction beat, satisfying value-added reveal, cold-water ending on the fraud.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and settle any VAT period — payable or refund — in one subtraction.
